newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: CA deadline passes, Bank Austria ups bid.
newsitem.headline: CA deadline passes, Bank Austria ups bid.

text.p: A final deadline for bidders in the race for Austrian privatisation candidate Creditanstalt expired on Friday as expectations grew the winner for the flagship bank may be announced at the weekend.
"We can't say anything. (Finance Minister Viktor) Klima is deliberating with his advisors," a source inside the finance ministry told Reuters.
Klima gave three bidders for the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt until 0800 GMT on Friday to improve their existing offers.
Market leader Bank Austria, who Klima said had made the highest bid at 16.7 billion schillings ($1.5 billion), on Friday said it had raised its offer further.
"Bank Austria has improved its offer," a bank spokesman told Reuters, but declined to be drawn on any details of the adjusted offer.
The domestic news agency APA reported Klima was expected to release a statement on his next steps by midday. Nobody in the finance ministry was immediately available for confirmation.

The Austrian daily Der Standard quoted sources close to Klima as saying he was likely to announce the future owner of Austria's flagship bank after an emergency session of leaders of the embattled government coalition, which has been deeply divided over the sale.
A special parliamentary session on the sale has been called for Tuesday, and Klima is widely expected to make his choice known before that day.

The dominant Social Democrats want the bank to be sold to main rival Bank Austria, while their junior partner, the conservative People's Party, prefer a bid by a consortium led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali.

Observers widely expect Bank Austria, which leads the consortium's bid by some three billion schillings, to be picked as Creditanstalt's new owner, raising the spectre of a major shake-up in Austria's overcrowded financial sector.
But the growing political controversy over the sale has cast a shadow over the fractious government partnership.

The conservative's threat to team up with the far-right opposition to sour a possible deal for Bank Austria by forcing it to pay an extra several billion schillings to small shareholders threatens to derail their fragile partnership with the Social Democrats of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky.

Vranitzky told Austrian state radio on Friday he was convinced the coalition would survive the biggest crisis in its one-year history. "Nobody, including the (People's Party) is seriously questioning the coalition," he said. ($ = 11.10 Austrian Schillings)
